speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after five weeks of explanation, the hon. member does not understand yet that what we did in the budget was reduce the federal income tax for all taxpayers across the land, with an agreement with the provinces, except Quebec, that they were to increase their provincial income tax and with the proceeds were to cut their sales tax, on an agreed formula. subsubtopic: EXTRADITION PROVISIONS IN BILL S-8
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, It was my intention to have the bill recalled before the committee in order to explain those clauses which seem to have been grossly misunderstood in the committee. The clause makes it very clear that this matter is discretionary. It is drawn in line with modern extradition arrangements and with the wording that prevails in the Commonwealth, which is standard practice in the European community in respect of extradition and is embodied in a number of our treaties. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: TABLING OF EXTRACT OF MINUTES OF MEETING OF COMMISSIONERS OF INTERNAL ECONOMY RESPECTING SALARY REVISIONS
speechtext:
Order, please. Before moving to routine proceedings I should like to state that the matter of salaries for the staff of the House of Commons has been one which has been in my hands for quite some time. Ordinarily in each year we have endeavoured to bring forward the Minute of the Commissioners of Internal Economy, who bear ultimate responsibility for salary changes, by April 1.
This year we endeavoured to address ourselves to the continuing problem arising from disparities between positions in the House of Commons and those in the public service. It was generally agreed that disparity ought not to occur and that, in fact, as much as possible, uniformity ought to exist between relative positions in the service of the House of Commons and in the public service.
The House will understand and recall that the House is autonomous in this regard and, therefore, approval of Treasury Board has not been sought on this or on previous occasions. However, there has always been a desire on the part of the House to conform as much as possible with the general ambitions and aims of the salary program in the public service, and to attempt to ensure that equivalent positions in the service of the House of Commons were maintained on a salary level either equivalent to or slightly ahead of those in the public service.
In attempting to do this we have, over the years, allowed some positions to get further ahead of equivalent positions in the public service than was desirable, and for this reason it has
Point of Order-Mr. Woolliams always been an ambition in respect of salary amendment arrangements each year to try to bring them closer into line. On the other hand, to attempt to do that in one year would always, it would seem to me and, I am sure, to all hon. members, unfairly burden those incumbents of positions in the service of the House of Commons.
I think all of us are generally agreed that the service rendered to the House of Commons by our staff at every level, by some 2,500 employees, is absolutely first-class and of top quality.
To take an approach in any one year which would place all the burden of this on any one incumbent or group of incumbents in our service of the House of Commons would mean an unfair program. Therefore an effort was made, and this is the reason the discussions have been rather longer and more complex than in other years, to find a formula which would at one and the same time recognize the need for fair salary treatment for those in incumbent positions, and yet draw closer into line those positions in the service of the House of Commons which have gone too far ahead of equivalent positions in the public service.
Accordingly, the opening of discussions related to the possibility of combining for the first time a percentage revision in respect of the positions themselves and a cash contribution to those incumbents who might, because of the necessity of a low percentage increase in their own classifications, be unfairly burdened. This is a new and rather complex approach, and it has taken some time to finalize it.
I am pleased to report to the House today, where a number of members have inquired, both on the floor of the House, through correspondence and in contact with me, on the progress, that the matter has been finalized. I have, of course, endeavoured to maintain a flow of information to the extent that was permitted, to the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services.
This matter has been finalized to my satisfaction, and I am, therefore, able also to say to the House that the Commissioners of Internal Economy have come to the same agreement. Therefore, I am able to table the minute of the Commissioners of Internal Economy touching upon salary revisions which, for the first time, and we hope this is a one and only time, include not only a percentage increase to the classifications of the salary groups in the House of Commons service, but also a once and for all cash payment which we hope very much reduces the burden on those who are present incumbents, yet recognizes the need to draw the general classifications closer in line with those in the public service. That minute is now final and official, and I table it forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, I reluctantly rise on a point of order, not to challenge your ruling, but rather to seek clarification regarding supplementary questions during the question period. I had a question for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) today which was of considerable
[Mr. Woolliams.l
importance. My supplementary would have been directed to the Acting Minister of National Revenue. My supplementary question is related to the fact that the Commerce Clearing House of Canada Limited is at present giving rulings across Canada which say that people who operate outside a family corporation, through a sale from a sibling, end up in a situation in which they are in fact unable to collect the tax supposed to be relieved by the minister's budget of April 10.
I would like to have clarification of what makes a supplementary question out of order. Is it simply the statement that the minister makes when that statement is yet unclear, or is there some automatic rule that means a person does not get a supplementary when asking a preliminary question?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member raises a very valid point of concern and one that gives the Chair great difficulty. In the question period today, and on many other days, there were and are occasions on which I grant members supplementary questions, and some which I do not. In the hon. member's case a question was put which clearly sought an opinion on an interpretation of a section of the law, and it is very difficult to permit such a matter to be followed up when in fact the minister recognizes and indicates that advice will have to be taken before an answer can be given.
It is very difficult for the Chair to grant a supplementary question on an answer that is to be deferred until some other time. On occasions where a minister has said it is a matter of investigation, not so much legal advice but merely investigation, 1 extend the benefit of the doubt to the member because I know that the member will want to say, "While the minister is undertaking the investigation which he has promised to the House, will he please pursue certain specifics that I have in mind?" Even at that point I will allow it to be pursued, but in today's case the hon. member put a question which clearly sought an opinion from the minister, and the minister's response was that he would have to obtain advice for the opinion. It is very difficult for me to permit that matter to be followed.
If the hon. member, in fact, had had a specific question about a particular bulletin-and 1 do say this to members generally-often members are tempted to try to set up a question of a specific nature with a question of a general nature. That may be a temptation for some purposes which members have in mind. In fact, in terms of the limited time available in the question period, it is a very counter productive practice.
If the hon. member's main concern today was a bulletin of a specific nature in the authority of the hon. minister for revenue, it might have been more advisable to make that the preliminary question which clearly would have been the subject of a supplementary. However, he began with a question seeking an opinion, and the minister indicated he would have to take advice before giving the opinion. Therefore, it seemed to me I did not have the choice to permit him to pursue it in that particular way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
That this House deeply regrets the inadequate response of the government to the persistent violation of international human rights, and in particular the violation by the Soviet Union and the Communist bloc of the Helsinki Accords.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to initiate this debate on a subject of very real and direct concern to the people of Canada. I am sure, even though this is a short sitting day in the House of Commons, that my motion will draw an active response from members on all sides of the House.
I am particularly honoured and pleased that this motion has been seconded by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: 1 think that no member of this House, and indeed no citizen of this country, has been more steadfast in his dedication to the cause of human rights in this country and throughout the world. That dedication was recognized last month by the extraordinary award of an honorary degree by the Ukrainian Free University in Munich to the right hon. member for Prince Albert, and it is symbolized further by the Canadian Bill of Rights which that member brought to parliament as Prime Minister.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
It is well for us to start the debate on human rights in Canada with reference fo the Canadian Bill of Rights. One of the basic principles enunciated in that bill is as follows:
Men and institutions remain free only when freedom is founded upon respect for moral and spiritual values and the rule of law.
That is a statement of principle for Canada in a bill that applies to Canada. Our first responsibility as legislators in this country is to strive to ensure its respect and application in our own country. Indeed, the degree to which we succeed in this

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
regard will, in a very real measure, speak to our capacity to pursue the cause of human rights in the world.
That principle is not limited to Canada-it is a declaration for mankind-and we in this House, we in this country should never be reticent or apologetic in our effort to have these principles accepted and respected by all nations and all peoples throughout the world. Certainly we have made some progress in that regard, but it is slow progress and it is uneven. There remain far too many countries and far too many governments for whom respect for individual freedoms is a meaningless phrase and for whom terror and suppression are the daily tools of their power. That is particularly true of countries of the Soviet bloc. The evidence of that fact is no further removed than today's press reports of the arbitrary arrest of Czech citizens prominent in the field of human rights, for no nobler purpose than to avoid any potential embarrassment for the visiting Soviet leader, Mr. Brezhnev. The fact is very much alive, too, in the hearts and minds of thousands of Canadians who themselves suffered in the past under these repressive regimes, and whose relatives and friends continue today to be denied even the most elementary rights and freedoms.
I do not want to enter a long catalogue, but I think there are some of these restrictions, limitations and suppression of freedom to which it is important we give specific attention in this House today.
Not long ago I raised in this House, as did other members, including the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leg-gatt), the case of Mr. Danylo Shumuk, who at 62 years of age had spent almost 35 years in prison for an assortment of crimes, mostly political, against the Soviet Union. That definition can cover almost anything. Relatives of Mr. Shumuk in Canada enlisted my support to see if Mr. Shumuk could leave the Soviet Union to emigrate to Canada. We were told that the Soviet Union does not view Mr. Shumuk's case as viable under the family unification provisions of the Helsinki Accord because his relatives in Canada are not sons and daughters but, rather, cousins. This is a narrow, legalistic interpretation designed to suit the purposes of the Soviet Union and not the humanitarian goals of the countries signatory to the Helsinki Accord.
We are seeing an easing of religious persecution in some countries within the Soviet bloc-Poland is the best example. But there is still a long way to go. Other countries in the Soviet bloc, Czechoslovakia is the most prominent, take active measures to prevent the free worship by its citizens in the religion of their choice.
There is also, as we know, the problem of emigration of Soviet Jews to Israel. The record of the government of the Soviet Union in one of harassment of those seeking to leave- of putting in place unnecessary road blocks. It is one where the doctrine of fairness is not allowed to exist, where families are separated, because one member is allowed to emigrate but another is not.
[ Translation]
What makes these violations of human rights so awful is the fact that Soviet Union authorities are not willing to respect the provisions of the Helsinki Agreement. The Secretary of State for External Affairs says that this agreement as well as others signed by the Soviet Union have no legal authority and that they cannot therefore be forcibly enforced. This is true, but it is also true that no country, including the Soviet Union, was forced to sign a single agreement ensuring the respect of human rights. When they signed these agreements, countries like the Soviet Union committed themselves in principle. Mr. Speaker, countries such as Canada must constantly remind violators of the contents of agreements such as that of Helsinki. This is the mistake that is being made in the foreign policy of Canada: there is too much reluctance and unwillingness to speak plainly.
It is always easier for us to turn our attention away from violations of freedom and dignity, particularly when those violations occur in other lands. If we in Canada indulge in that luxury we leave those who are victims of oppression in the world without defenders, because there are other countries, including other countries in the west, which rely more exclusively on Soviet trade or whose populations might be subject to unusual pressures, and are consequently less free than Canada is to speak up.
We in this parliament must face the fact that if countries like Canada and the United States of America do not play a leading role in speaking up for human rights in this world, then no one else will.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: The reticence of the Government of Canada in accepting that obligation is often justified by reference to so-called quiet diplomacy; the claim that human rights issues are best pursued quietly and privately with other governments. That may well be the proper case in negotiations on individual cases, particularly concerning the reunification of families. But we on this side of the House of Commons reject any notion that the Government of Canada should be quiet in its commitment to the principles of human rights.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
That commitment does not belong in the back rooms of diplomacy. It should be set forth clearly and publicly by this government so that the people of Canada, and the nations of the world, know exactly where this country stands.
Without that kind of public evidence of the government's commitment to human rights Canadians will be entitled to suspect that quiet diplomacy is just some kind of evasion, some kind of a cop-out. Particularly will that be the case when we have a government, as we have today, which has shown so little
[Mr. Clark.)
May 31, 1978

concern for the fundamental rights and freedoms of its own citizens.
It is important for us to turn some attention for a moment as we discuss our impact upon human rights in the world to consider the impact of the example of Canada in terms of respect for rights in this country. In this country we have a government that tried to gag a member of this House with threats, and having failed there, is now harassing a newspaper editor whom it does not happen to like. This is a government, and we heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) on this subject only yesterday, that condones secret trials. This is a government that continues to use writs of assistance 200 years after they were abolished in England. This is a government that, as we saw again today, is all too ready to take away from parliament and hide, with a royal commission, responsibility for looking into the illegal use of the private tax and medical files of individual Canadians.
This is a government which wants to inhibit the basic freedoms of charitable organizations by limiting their right to petition their government and their parliament. This is a government that finds no fault with the systematic surveillance of political parties and candidates. This is a government that passed an order in council making it illegal for any Canadian even to discuss the activities of a uranium cartel, of which the Government of Canada was a part. This is a government which, under the Immigration Act, claims the right to give foreign workers in Canada a special social insurance number so they can be singled out.
This is a government which increases postal rates by executive fiat, in defiance of the law and in defiance of parliamentary principle. When Canadians look at a record like that we are entitled to ask ourselves: is this government so committed to quiet diplomacy in the defence of human rights internationally because quiet diplomacy works, or because it is a convenient way to evade action and avoid scrutiny?
If this government has been too silent in asserting Canada's commitment to human rights, it most certainly has been inconsistent and hypocritical in applying those principles to its own policies. On occasion we hear lofty statements of principle on this matter by government ministers. We heard one in the House of Commons last December made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) when he was talking about commercial relations with South Africa. We noted, to give him credit-and he is in the House now-the strong statement of the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Cafik) in summing up the tragic failure of the Belgrade Conference. We heard a statement in recent days from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in respect of our aid policy toward Cuba. The rhetoric in these statements is fine. The record unfortunately, does not measure up.
To take some of those examples, we are told that the government is ending its support of commercial dealings with South Africa. But the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) sees nothing wrong with the Export Development Corporation continuing to support activity in that country. Indeed, he gives us to understand that his
Human Rights
concern for human rights begins and ends with credit ratings. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), when he finally understood the arrangement he had made, was happy to have South African banks participate in propping up the Canadian dollar. The Prime Minister's statement in regard to Cuba was just as empty. He made the grandiose gesture of cutting off aid that in fact had already stopped. Even after that statement in relation to Cl DA, the fact is the Export Development Corporation continues to finance sales to the Castro regime.
The government would have us believe that it is concerned about the massive repression of civil liberties in Chile, and yet it continues to support commercial dealings with that regime. An all-party group of members from this House, as you will recall, reported evidence of terror and suppression in Argentina, and the government sold that country one Candu reactor and tries to sell it another.

Even though the resolutions introduced in the House concerning Mr. Shcharansky and Mr. Orlov received unanimous consent, it is obvious that the government does not take these matters seriously. Even though there was agreement to give unanimous consent, we are not doing enough to follow up on the statements made in parliament. It seems that we are not using these statements. Moreover, the government does not express steadfastly enough its concern about cases such as those I have mentioned. They are usually put aside and quickly forgotten.
Canada should take the initiative and raise at the United Nations the obvious cases of violation of human rights. A few weeks ago, the House of Commons agreed unanimously to a motion by the hon. member for Matane (Mr. De Bane), supported by my colleague from Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), about the Shcharansky case. I then proposed that this motion serve as a starting point for a Canadian initiative at the United Nations. Nothing has been done in this regard, but the proposal is still valid and I hope it will receive serious consideration.
Canada should also reveal and publicize the violations of human rights in other countries. We should not allow the continuation of current repressions in Chile, in Latin America, in Indonesia and in South Africa without objecting to them.
In sum, this is a government whose commitment is doubtful and whose record is shabby. The people of Canada expect better of their government in support of human rights. I say to this House and to the people of Canada that the government we form after the next election will provide a better example and a better quality of life.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
First, we will put our own domestic house in better order. A government which believed in freedom of

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
information for its own citizens would have more credibility in asserting the rights of citizens of other countries. A government prepared to rewrite an outdated and frighteningly vague Official Secrets Act, and to end the use of ill-defined procedures like writs of assistance, will be a stronger voice for human rights in the world. We will take those initiatives.
Second, we will never be quiet about our commitment to the principles of fundamental liberties for all mankind. We will assert that commitment at every opportunity, and back it up with concrete international action. Our government, for example, will be an active, not a passive, supporter of the appointment of a United Nations Commissioner of Human Rights.
Third, we will apply the principles to which all Canadians are committed, openly and consistently. We will not provide Canadian aid to governments guilty of gross violation of human rights, and we will not use agencies like the EDC to do by the back door what we condemn at the front door.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Fourth, we will be both forthright and realistic in our recognition of the motives of the Soviet Union. The kindest thing one can say about this government in relation to the Soviet Union is that it is remarkably naive about the motives of that country.
The Prime Minister's external affairs adviser confesses he would have liked to have kept the lid on the most recent example of Soviet espionage in Canada because he was worried how the Soviet government might react if the people of Canada were told about it. When that same case came to light, the Prime Minister sought to downplay it because he said he was concerned about its impact on our trade with the Soviet Union. And now this week we have our Prime Minister virtually isolated among NATO leaders in his apparent lack of any serious concern about the continuing build-up of Warsaw Pact forces in central Europe.
Canada's national interest is ill-served by such naivete. The Soviet Union will continue to buy our grain and other products because it needs them, and because we are able to supply them at the right time and right price. That is the essence of Soviet commercial policy, and no amount of pussy-footing around on spies or human rights will change it. As for the Soviet build-up in central Europe and its expanding activity in Africa, what is required of Canada and all NATO countries is not to turn a blind eye, but to respond forcefully and effectively, as proposed by President Carter and President Giscard d'Estaing.
Finally, and most important, we will make our commitment to human rights a legitimate priority in formulating Canadian foreign policy, as is the case in the United States.
I began with references to the Bill of Rights. The principles set forth so eloquently by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert in the Bill of Rights are real. They embody the most essential beliefs of our society, of our very raison d'etre as a nation, and Canadians have a right to expect that these real principles have real meaning in the policies of their government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
First, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to thank the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) for his generous words concerning myself. At the same time, I express my fear at the number of ministers who are here this afternoon of a government as multitudinous as the sands of the sea, a cabinet that has been multiplied in numbers.
A matter is before the House of transcendent interest to all who believe in freedom, and the total number of ministers present is three. That indicates the attitude of this government and the degree to which fundamental freedoms have been undermined, to an extent never before known in my day, and I have been here for a long while. A number of examples were set forth by the Leader of the Opposition.
Where is Canada going? That question is in the hearts and minds of Canadians everywhere today. What about human rights and fundamental freedoms? What about international rights set out in agreements solemnly entered into by the U.S.S.R., and as solemnly disregarded? It is that I am going to speak about in particular today.
1 simply want to make a general reference to an honour that came to me. The Leader of the Opposition made reference to an honorary degree from the Ukrainian Free University in Munich, Germany, a university composed of men and women who, in the interests of freedom, have been forced out of their own countries and are endeavouring to keep alive the fire of freedom.
1 want to mention particularly Dr. W. Yaniw, the Rector, and Dr. Sakaluk, the Pro-Rector, who came to Saskatoon for the purpose of joining in that award which, of the many I have received throughout the years, none has touched me more deeply.
From the time that we went to western Canada to the Northwest Territories, in 1903, to Carlton, I saw something of the injustice being done to those of racial origin other than the two basic races. 1 saw shocking examples of discrimination on the basis of race and colour. I determined when I was only ten or 11 that I would devote my life to bringing an end in this nation to discrimination on the basis of race, colour, or otherwise.

Each one of us has in his or her heart something that no one else has, something placed there by the Almighty, it must be. They will be a minority who follow that something. Ultimately the minority will become a majority if what is being undertaken and tried is for the welfare of people in general.

The Leader of the Opposition mentioned that this government is noted for its quiet diplomacy. 1 certainly agree with the quietness. As far as the diplomacy is concerned, it has been a government that has refused to stand internationally and nationally.

As far as the French language is concerned, it is sometimes forgotten that I had the largest support in the province of Quebec any Conservative leader had received since the days of Macdonald. It was on the basis of the stand I had taken in 1921. As a young lawyer I was asked whether 1 would take an appeal order which was made in the trial of two French Canadian trustees, Boutin and Ethier, who had been convicted of permitting the teaching of French beyond the extent contemplated by the law. Everybody knew my objective was parliament. My friends came to me and said, "If you take that case you can never hope to be in parliament." And they almost proved it. In other words, believing in freedom and the maintenance of those principles in the constitution without which Canada cannot survive, I took trial after trial when it was not popular to do so.

Where are we going? I brought a question before parliament just before Helsinki. I will not read it in detail. I asked the question on July 24, 1975. I said:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Next week there will be a meeting of 35 nations in Helsinki. We in this House have no idea whatsoever as to the stand that the Prime Minister will take on behalf of Canada, there having been no day set aside for the purpose of discussion and ascertaining the feelings of members of this House with regard to the tremendous problems affecting the peace of not only Europe, but of the world, which will come up. That committee is dedicated to freedom, stands for freedom, and maintains courage at all times in that connection.
I specifically ask the Prime Minister .. . whether any treaty signed by Canada should include a definite commitment by all signatories, including the U.S.S.R., to implement within their jurisdictions the principles embodied in the universal declaration of human rights and, second, that in the establishment of boundaries in eastern Europe which are the result of conquest, that such establishment should be conditional on the principle of self-determination being accepted by the U.S.S.R. and the other nations. They are very concerned-
They wanted to know what was going to take place. That is a summary of what I asked. The Prime Minister answered, with the usual clarity which characterizes him when he endeavours to conceal completely what this House wants to know. He said:

Mr. Speaker, I did not interrupt the right hon. gentleman while he was speaking because of my respect for him as a human being. 1 will deal with his question if the right hon. gentleman will exercise a little patience.
The second point 1 want to make is in relation to a comment made by the Leader of the Opposition, who seems to feel that members of this government or of this party have a naive attitude toward the Soviet Union and perhaps other countries which violate human rights. I certainly do not have any naive impression as to the motivation or the idealogical differences in regime between some of those countries and others in the world, including Canada. Canada is a democratic society with a very strong base, historically and presently, of respect for human rights. It is evident that other regimes of this world do not have such an attitude or disposition, and we suffer no naivete about that whatsoever.
The other suggestion which was made by the Leader of the Opposition, which I felt hit a little below the belt and which, to my knowledge, has no foundation in fact, related to the expulsion of Soviet spies from Canada. If I interpreted the hon. member's remarks correctly, he seemed to want to leave the implication that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would rather have dealt with that quietly.
That is a strange, anomalous position to be taken by the Leader of the Opposition who, on the other hand, often seems to think that the Prime Minister makes all the decisions. In this particular case the Leader of the Opposition seems to think that the Prime Minister was overruled. The fact is that the decision to expel Soviet spies was made by the cabinet of Canada. The Prime Minister, myself, all other cabinet ministers and members on this side of the House unanimously support that decision, in spite of ramifications which may result regarding Soviet-Canadian relations. We do not want spies of any country in this country, and we took steps which any self-respecting government would take. We are not naive in this respect either.
The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert, for whom I have a great deal of respect, wanted to know what happened regarding numerous motions under Standing Order 43. I would like to say that my respect for the House of Commons, to my knowledge, has not been challenged very often, if at all. When 1 was in Belgrade, in my speech on behalf of the Government of Canada, I referred to unanimous resolutions of the House of Commons, in order to substantiate the strong position we were taking, and to indicate that all Canadians, through their elected representatives, unanimously supported that strong, hard stand in relation to human rights. Also I

delivered personally to Ambassador Veronsof the resolution which was passed in the House of Commons in respect of the human rights issue. Just prior to my departure, I had that delivered directly to him.

There is no question whatsoever as to our position in relation to this. I draw the attention of hon. members opposite and the people of Canada to the fact that unanimous resolutions have been passed by the House on a variety of human rights issues. Some of them have been brought forward by hon. members of the opposition, some of them have been brought forward by hon. members of the government. All of the resolutions relating to this subject, to my knowledge, have been supported unanimously. There is more to unite us on this issue of human rights, if we were to set aside the partisan political considerations which perhaps motivate some people in their comments.
The other point which was made by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) relates to the Helsinki Final Act itself. He seems to feel that it was a bad thing to enter into. He may well adopt whatever position he likes. When the agreement was originally signed, there were some who felt, as he apparently does, that the signing of the Final Act solidified existing boundaries in Europe.
On December 19, 1977 in my speech in the House of Commons, I dealt with this question in a similar debate. I indicated, as is the fact, that there is no solidification or moral sanction of the existing boundaries in eastern Europe. There is nothing in the Final Act which in fact does that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext: That is simply not correct.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
It does indicate that the signatory countries will not use force to change the existing boundaries. That is altogether different than giving moral sanction to those boundaries, or to say that we, as a government, or any other signatory government, support that particular position.
I should like to refer to the motion directly. I am the first to agree that it is unfortunately true that there still exist all too many serious violations of human rights in many countries, violations which are a proper cause of concern to many Canadians. However, I find it difficult to understand, let alone accept, how this government can be accused of inadequacy in its response to these situations. For the record, I shall now outline what positive actions this government has taken in the international human rights field. In this context, 1 will deal with the more specific issue of the U.S.S.R., the Helsinki accords, the Belgrade conference and its aftermath.
Whether at the United Nations General Assembly, in multilateral fora such as the United Nations Commission on Human Rights and the recent Belgrade meeting, as well as in our bilateral relationships with a number of countries, Canada has expressed clearly and vigorously its concern with violations

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
of human rights, and has acted positively to resolve such issues.
At the United Nations we have joined with other like-minded countries in developing and sponsoring a series of resolutions which expressed the condemnation of the international community with regard to the persistent and often appalling violation of human rights in countries such as South Africa and Chile. As well, we have been involved at the United Nations in efforts to eliminate all forms of racial discrimination, torture, other cruel, inhumane and degrading treatment of persons, and of religious intolerance. In all, over 30 different aspects of human rights are currently being dealt with by the United Nations General Assembly, and Canada has played a prominent role in this important forum.
At the most recent thirty-fourth session of the United Nations Commission on Human Rights in February, Canada's delegation to that 34-member body was active in having the commission deal with a variety of human rights situations throughout the world, including Cambodia. As hon. members will recall, the commission's call upon Cambodia to explain its human rights record was cited in the resolution of April 7 of this House which condemned Cambodia. As well, the United Nations Commission dealt with the human rights situation in South Africa, Chile, Argentina, Uganda, Uruguay, Indonesia, Paraguay, Bolivia, the Republics of Korea, and Ethiopia. The human rights situation in the U.S.S.R. was raised by several delegations, including that of Canada. Our delegation brought to the commission's attention the unanimous resolution of the House with regard to the Shcharansky case.
Although the work of the United Nations does not always make the headlines and has no enforcement machinery, it is nevertheless a principal channel for bringing the weight of international opinion to bear on countries which persistently violate human rights. After an active campaign following the thirty-fourth session of the commission, Canada was recently re-elected by the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations to another three-year term on the commission in an open election, the results of which clearly reflected the high regard for Canada among the international community for our work on that important body. It is now our intention to continue to work to broaden the commission's scope and to improve its methods of work so as to ensure that it is made as effective an international instrument as possible.
Unfortunately there is no international consensus in the United Nations on many human rights subjects or situations, and no effective enforcement machinery. However, this does not mean that Canada will slacken its efforts at the United Nations, since that body does express considerable public opinion which in many areas, and for some violations, can be effective.

The situations in Cambodia, Chile, Uganda, South Africa, and the cases of Shcharansky and Orlov, are only a few of those which have been of concern to the government. That concern has been reinforced by many members on both sides of the House, particularly those members involved in the human rights work of the joint parliamentary committee. Also it reflects the interests of Amnesty International, other nongovernmental organizations, and individual Canadians who have written to the government, ministers, and other members, to express their concerns and views.
In my own particular case I have received representations from the ethnocultural communities across Canada. 1 have met with them by the hundreds and thousands to deal with our human rights' stance and position. Without fear of contradiction, the position I have taken in respect of this particular equation and very central human question has drawn enormous support in this country. I am deeply grateful for that support of my expression of the views of Canadians on these very important issues.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Having dealt with the question of Canada's responses to violations of human rights in a number of countries, both through multilateral and bilateral channels, now I should like to turn to the specific aspect of the motion before us which deals with the Soviet Union, the communist bloc countries, and the Helsinki Final Act.
The response of the government regarding the way the human rights provisions of the Helsinki Final Act are being implemented by the U.S.S.R. and the Eastern European participants is based on two main considerations: first, the constraints imposed on us by the nature of the Final Act itself. It is a set of guidelines without any deadlines or any hard and fast rules as to how its provisions are to be implemented. There is no doubt there is a moral and political commitment rather than a legal one, and in my view an international commitment according to a very sacred document. The second is in respect of what action will be most effective in achieving our main objective, which is to improve the situation of those who suffer as a result of deficiencies in the respect being shown to the human rights provision of that Act.
Those who have taken the time to read the booklet "Canada at Belgrade", that was recently published by the Department of External Affairs, and which has been distributed to all
May 31, 1978

members of this House, will be well aware of the firm position of the Canada delegation at Belgrade.
I think our position was the envy of many countries of the world. There is no doubt whatsoever that it has evoked considerable concern on the part of the Soviet Union and many countries of Eastern Europe. I am not sure I am unique in this respect, and I certainly know that a former Prime Minister of this country, the right hon. member for Prince Albert, in his days as Prime Minister had the distinction and the honour of being attacked by the Soviet Union for some of his very tough stands, but 1 was very pleased the other day to note that in Kiev, in an official communist organ, a whole page was devoted to what I think was a slanderous attack, but quite accurate in some respects, on my position regarding human rights. If I can be attacked in that substantive way, 1 must be doing something right.
It is very difficult to end up building a case that this government has been weak on this issue, if in fact those countries are very much concerned with the tough stand we have taken and go to the trouble in a foreign country of attacking myself, particularly, because of the strong stance 1 have taken.
There is more than just words, of course, in relation to the human rights equation. We have to do more than just talk. We have to try to realize some positive achievements. There is talk here in this House and in the country as to the virtues of quiet diplomacy versus the virtues of taking an open, hard line stance in order to focus public opinion on these violations of human rights.
There is no question but that in individual cases the quiet approach is often the more successful. The statistics would indicate that this government, through the approach it has taken on individual human rights violations, has indeed achieved some marked success. 1 do not think we should take the risk of losing those opportunites to be successful simply for the polemics of the thing. Perhaps from time to time we have to move in both directions. The stance 1 have personally taken as the minister of multiculturalism could perhaps be categorized as less than quiet diplomacy. Quiet diplomacy has a valid position as well in order that we can maximize our opportunity of achieving success.
In Belgrade our position was strong. There the final document that emanated from Belgrade was a considerable disappointment to all the participants. It was a disappointment, I think, to all Canadians and all freedom loving people in the world. The fact is it was a consensus document. It does provide some hope that in two years down the line in Madrid, where there will be a second follow up conference, this government and other like-minded governments will be able to zero in again on human rights violations that still remain.
I am very hopeful that as long as we continue to conduct dialogue and talk between the two ideological camps of this world, dealing with these questions in an open and frank way, and continuing to insist that the application and implementation of the Final Act is a matter of public concern to this government, and a matter of international right for us to
Human Rights
express our views in respect of it, there is the possibility that change will come.
Change cannot come quickly, not because we would not want it so but because the simple fact is that the question of human rights within the Soviet Union and other countries in that part of the world boils down to a very basic and fundamental thing. It is felt perhaps by many of those countries in positions of authority that the giving of the kind of freedom that we enjoy and take for granted would destroy the very nature of their countries. I think they may well be right. It is for that reason it is difficult to move them to the kind of respect for human rights that is so inherent within our society. We must understand that, we must have patience, and we must never be reluctant to speak out powerfully and forcefully on behalf of all people anywhere in the world whose rights have been violated. That is my position and the position of this government, and it will continue to be the position of this government on behalf of all people all over the world.

The last point I would like to make, and I think it is very serious, is that two years down the road there will be a second follow up conference at Madrid on security and co-operation in Europe. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my party I would like to say at the outset that the subject matter of this motion, which expresses regret, according to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), that the government's response to the persistent violations of human rights, particularly violations of the Helsinki Agreement by countries within the Soviet bloc, is a matter of very real importance. This subject touches upon, quite correctly, the issue of human liberty, and it is one that a demoncratic assembly, whether in Canada or anywhere else in the world, ought to regard as being of great importance, because liberty is not something that ought to be restricted as a value to a

particular country in which one happens to live as a matter of moral concern.
Human liberty is a matter not only of concern for Canadians but for all men and women throughout the world. It may have been preferable to include in the motion a reference to the denial of liberties in non-Soviet bloc countries, and I am thinking of Chile and Argentina. I was pleased to see the opposition leader make reference to authoritarian regimes of a kind other than those found in the Soviet bloc. I merely say in passing that it might have been useful in other circumstances to have a motion that pertains to human liberty universal in its application to all those regimes in the world where human liberties are denied, whether it is the Soviet bloc or somewhere else.
However, the issue before us today is the Soviet bloc, its denial of liberty, and the response that this government has or has not given to that question. I am in a bit of a dilemma, Mr. Speaker, and I say this candidly as a democrat, socialist, and Canadian, in coming to grips directly with this question. It is one thing to talk about what one can do within one's own state or one's society at a given time in order to achieve human liberty for one's own people or one's own community. The question we are really debating today, if I understand it correctly, is really what can one nation state do about influencing the development of liberty in another nation state. It is a difficult question, and anyone who is concerned about war and peace, and about civilized relationships between nations, as well as human liberty for people within a nation, has to come to grips with it.
We cannot simply rely on rhetoric or eloquent phrases about the need to promote liberty in other nation states. One has to come to grips with this serious question, when talking about national politics, of the limitations, if they exist, and the course of action that is open to one nation state believing in liberty, in terms of its effect on achieving liberty for individuals in other states where that liberty is being denied. This is the basic concern that we should be facing in this debate.
One of the elementary ways that a country, whether it is Canada or any other country, can demonstrate its concern about liberty and basic rights is to demonstrate, with unequivocal commitment, with unequivocal day to day action, its own demonstrable belief in liberty by practising that at home and by preserving and ensuring that the practices of freedom where they exist are maintained.
I have not been impressed by the present government's commitment to the basic principles of civil liberty as reflected in our systems, as they pertain directly to the principle of the rule of law. The minister who just sat down coined one of the great abominations in terms of language of politics in this decade not many months ago when he said, "From time to time in Canada the rule of reason ought to replace the rule of law." Anyone who knows about the rule of law and what it means in this country would shudder, I am sure, when they heard that abomination coming from that minister in the context of a serious debate about the limitations of the actions of the RCMP and the appropriate response of ministers of the

Crown in exercising control over the RCMP. That whole issue has, in the view of myself and every person in this country who is concerned with liberties-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
The hon. member has certainly demonstrated in the clearest possible way his attitude of having the rule of reason replace the rule of law, for if ever there was a non-point of order, that was it. There is no one, Mr. Speaker, who misunderstood the minister's remarks at the time, and I say that not as a cheap shot to a particular minister in this instance, but the whole ministry, as at the time-the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) and the minister for multiculturalism (Mr. Cafik)-it showed at the peak period of the debate about the mishandling of internal security matters by this government a shoddy respect for the whole principle of the rule of law, a shoddy neglect of the importance of preserving civil liberties. I have no intention of documenting that today, because we are on another matter.
I am saying that in any democracy one way of demonstrating clearly your own commitment to the principles of liberty is to practise that at home, and that is not what we have had in an unequivocal fashion from this government.
I would like now to shift to the other part of the motion which makes specific reference to the Soviet bloc countries. Mr. Speaker, at the end of my remarks I will deal with what I think are severe limitations in a nation state having an effect on the liberty of other countries. One of the things that we can do and should do from time to time, not in any state of self righteousness but hopefully because it reflects our commitment to the age old notion of human liberty, is bear witness to what is actually going on in other countries in the world.
Every speech about freedom should not merely be political rhetoric of a self-serving nature. From time to time world
Human Rights
leaders, prime ministers and others, have an obligation-as I think President Carter has demonstrated in the past couple of years-to speak out about liberty beyond the borders of their own nations and to give visible evidence of its denial, to show visible concern to the people within other states and to say that the situation ought to be rectified.
There is no doubt in my mind that the Helsinki Accord, which was ratified by the heads of 35 states three years ago, has been violated in a serious way by countries in the Soviet bloc. The expectations that were generated at the outset of the revolution in the Soviet Union at the conclusion of the first world war were for the emancipation of people in that part of the world in the fullest possible way. What we have seen is a regime, from Lenin on, that has imposed perhaps the most restrictive and coercive set of bureaucratic, to use a euphemism, practices which have denied human liberty.
There has been vivid demonstration of that in the works of Solzhenitsyn, and recently vivid and disturbing evidence has been brought forward that psychiatric practice even in the Soviet Union today is being used and perverted to equate discontent and criticism of the Soviet regime as visible demonstration of schizophrenia. It is being actively pursued by people who call themselves psychiatrists in the Soviet Union. It is a clear and utter abuse of the principles of human health sciences if there ever was one, Mr. Speaker.
There has been in the Soviet Union, of course, the persistent repression of cultural minorities. The Ukrainians stand out, perhaps, in our country as the largest group numerically. Many of us have been involved in individual cases of men and women who have dared to speak out simply for the right to emphasize their own cultural distinctiveness, their own uniqueness as part of the Soviet bloc. There is the case of Valentyn Moroz which is an outstanding example, but there have been many others. The reality is that the Soviet Union, preceding the Helsinki Agreement and post Helsinki, violates human rights in a way that is not acceptable to men and women anywhere who believe in the principles of freedom.
In the context of this motion I want to do what I think politicians in free societies ought to do from time to time, and that is to talk about a particular event that is going on that demonstrates the perversion of the principles of human liberty. In this particular instance I want to talk about that beautiful, exciting, creative country on the one hand, but also sad and deeply disturbing country on the other, namely, Czechoslovakia.
There have been few countries in modern history that have had the opportunity for the complete flowering of human liberty in all its aspects, including human equality, that compare with Czechoslovakia. It is a small country in the heart of Europe, highly industrialized, highly creative in the arts, highly developed in all the early principles of liberal democracy. In cycles beginning in 1938, then 1968-and I think in 1978 we are going to witness it again-it has had experiences of a particular cataclysmic nature that have denied the flowering of human liberty in that country. This is what a lot of us, experiencing and watching the development of mankind in this

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
century, had hoped would not take place. We had hoped to see a more positive and creative society emerge.
Just over a year ago in that remarkable country an 1,800-word statement was signed. It was a terse statement, relatively devoid of rhetoric, but moving because of that. It was signed initially by about 200 people in Czechoslovakia, and in it an appeal was made to the Czechoslovakian government, and beyond that to all the people of the world, to look at what was happening in the denial of basic human liberties in that land- the denial of free speech, of the right to worship, the right to privacy, and the right to due process of law.
In signing that the participants were making two claims, first, that the Helsinki Accord was being violated, and second, in terms of the principles allegedly maintained in the constitution of their own country, their rights were not being adhered to but were being denied. Signing that petition were liberals, socialists, communists, religious, and artistic people of no particular political persuasion. It represented a cross-section of the Czech community who wanted nothing more than basic human liberty. The statement itself was neither anti-state nor anti-socialist. It was produced by a group of people who were primarily fighting for the liberty of their fellow citizens.
Interestingly enough, the document was not written as an appeal for the freedom of that particular category usually described as intellectuals-novelists, musicians, university professors, lawyers and so on. It was concerned that the freedom that is being denied in Czechoslovakia, that is being denied today, is having its most regressive effects on the ordinary working people of that country.
One of the signers of that charter was a distinguished historian by the name of Karel Bartosek. In signing this document he drew attention to the fact that what was of particular concern to him and his friends was that ordinary disasters such as a mining disaster that had taken place in Czechoslovakia were not reported in the news because of censorship.
That is the point I want to make in my remarks today, Mr. Speaker, about the effects of the denial of freedom of expression in a country like Czechoslovakia, Romania, the Soviet Union, or any other country that denies freedom of expression. What they are doing is not simply curtailing the right of a handful of intellectuals to express their views, much more important in numerical terms is the fact that they are denying the right to have the problems of ordinary people, whether they be industrial workers or farmers, discussed and debated. That, basically, is what the charter of 1977 was all about.
Perhaps the most distinguished signatory of that charter was Professor Jan Patocka of Czechoslovakia, who is considered by many to be among the two or three outstanding philosophers in the history of that country. He was 69 when he signed it a year and four months ago, so it was a matter of considerable courage on his part. We can make speeches about other countries, but it takes no particular courage to do that. It took a lot of courage for this man to sign this document at the age of 69.
I want to quote what he said about the importance of liberty in a country like Czechoslovakia. He said:
Without a moral basis, without a conviction which does not stem from opportunity, circumstances or expected advantages, no society can function, regardless of how advanced it is technically ... (but) it is not man who defines a moral order according to arbitrary needs, wishes, tendencies and desires. On the contrary, it is morality which defines the man ... the notion of an international pact regarding human rights-
He was talking about the Helsinki Accord.
-means only this: societies place themselves under the sovereignty of a moral belief... It is to this conviction that Charter 77 is responding.
Just shortly after he signed that petition, within a matter of weeks, in part because of harassment that he received in the Czechoslovakian state, he died.
I notice that my time is just about up, but the point I want to make in this all too brief allusion to Czechoslovakia is that there are certain things we can do in a nation state that is apart from another nation state in which liberties are being denied. One is that from time to time we should describe that reality. I say in all seriousness that the Prime Minister has not been among world leaders in that respect, in my view. I do not recall the Prime Minister making a speech, either in the House of Commons or outside, on basic liberties, giving concrete examples where they are being denied in other states, where he has made an appeal to the international community to bring its moral force to bear in showing those people in other states that we care about their freedom. I would fault the Prime Minister on that score, because he should do more about it.

Mr. Speaker, I will continue. 1 want to thank my colleagues in the House for giving me extra time. I will not abuse that privilege and 1 will conclude my remarks very quickly.
I said that there was one area in which the nation state and politicians in that nation state can have an influence from time to time. It cannot be abused, but from time to time we have an obligation to speak out about the denial of liberty in other countries.
A second point I wanted to emphasize is that our best way of influencing liberty in other countries, without exaggerating our role and capacity to act on what happens in another state, is to practise those principles at home in order to give a visible demonstration that we intend to implement, within our own country, the principles of liberty about which we talk.
My final point concerns an issue touched upon by both the minister who spoke and the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). It was not fully developed, and it seems to me that it would be worth while pursuing it at another stage of this debate. In a world of nation states, what kinds of limited action can we take from the point of view of state power vis-a-vis another state? One suggestion which has been made in terms of other states that clearly violate human rights in an unequivocal way, pertains to aid programs. We should have nothing to do with aid programs for states in that kind of position. I agree with that. Beyond that minimal point, what can we do?
Can we close our doors to trade completely? Can we close our doors to other forms of human communication? I think not. We have to maintain some connection and communication. At least at the state to state level we can maintain some modicum of civilized existence, with the ultimate hope that the free societies, by demonstration of their freedom at home, will thus influence the development of freedom in other states.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-GOVERNMENT'S RESPONSE TO VIOLATION OF HUMAN RIGHTS BY SOVIET UNION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is rather refreshing to hear and follow the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) in this debate. He has evidently proven that it is possible to speak on this topic refraining from narrow partisan consideration and from exercising the kind of synthetic rage that was displayed earlier, at the beginning of the debate, by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark), followed by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). Both hon. members did not even take the trouble to attend the Belgrade conference and one really does not know whether they are in agreement or not.
If one looks for a moment at the wording of the motion before us today, which regrets "the inadequate response" of the Canadian government and criticizes it particularly in relation to violation by the Soviet Union and the communist bloc of the Helsinki Accord, one inevitably concludes that the Progressive Conservative party supports and agrees with the concept of the Helsinki Accord. Otherwise they would not
Human Rights
mention that Accord in their motion. Having done so, in the speech given by the right hon. member for Prince Albert, he comes pretty close to a rejection of the content and spirit and the objective of the Helsinki Accord. So we have the Leader of the Opposition using the Helsinki Agreement as a document against which we should measure our performance, and criticizing us for not having lived up to it, followed by one of his frontbenchers, perhaps not openly criticizing, but coming pretty close to expressing the thought that he has no time and no support for that very same agreement. If that is a display of unity in that party on a fundamental issue like this-

speechtext:
-on the sales tax we will be distracted on another occasion to demonstrate division on the other side as well. I would like to stick to the subject in the limited time available.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert displayed one of his old chestnuts which has been raised since the signing of the Helsinki Agreement, namely, saying this document in a way finalizes frontiers in Europe as inevitable, a conclusion about which nothing can be done. Nothing is further from the truth.
From the Helsinki Agreement Final Act at page 4, the second paragraph under the section headed "I. Sovereign equality, respect for the rights inherent in sovereignty" reads:
Within the framework of international law, all the participating States have equal rights and duties. They will respect each other's right to define and conduct as it wishes its relations with other States in accordance with international law and in the spirit of the present Declaration. They consider that their frontiers can be changed,-
And I repeat "can be changed".
It continues:
-in accordance with international law, by peaceful means and by agreement.
This is the point that does not seem to have been recognized, accepted, and perhaps even understood by the critics of the Helsinki Agreement.
Another criticism which was raised in the course of the debate earlier in the afternoon was one that related to the question that somehow, as a result of the Helsinki Agreement, free worship-I believe it was the Leader of the Official Opposition who made the criticism-has not been the subject of concern and has not been the subject of improvements in the ensuing years since 1975. I have news for the official opposition leader. If he had researched the subject matter before making his speech this afternoon, he would have learned that the representative of the Holy See made a speech in Belgrade on October 7, 1977. Monsignor Silvestrini made an intervention on behalf of the Holy See. I have a report of what he said about religious freedoms. It is only from one page that I will quote:
As regards religious freedoms it is an undeniable fact that the Final Act said "go" to this positive process although it is still at the start. This is, in particular,

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
sufficiently clear as regards circulation and meetings of persons and communications from country to country.
Indeed there have been confirmed encouraging developments in this field as far as we are concerned, by the various churches and various denominational groups. But in particular, as regards the Catholic church, of which I am particularly competent to speak, it is satisfying to note that a certain number of positive facts without doubt have been proved. Above all, there has been recorded a broader flow, a fairly steady one, of travel facilities for religious motives. Travel for bishops to come to Rome for their visit "ad limina" (as we know this is a visit which should be made every five years to the Pope by the bishops, and this year indeed it includes the turn of the European countries), or also for travel for bishops and other ecclesiastics to attend important meetings of the Holy See, or participation by monks and nuns in the general chapter of their order, or other conventions in Rome, or other places in Europe and America; or again, participation of bishops, priests, groups of the laiety in major international manifestations of a religious nature; like the Holy Year which took place at Rome in 1975, and the International Eucharistic Congress of Philadelphia in 1976-or for pilgrimages to European sanctuaries, both east and west. Furthermore we can note more frequent meetings and exchanges of visits among representatives of the Episcopy of various countries, more numerous concessions for priests who have emigrated to visit their own families at home, and a certain number of young ecclesiastics who have been sent to take study courses in cultural, theological university institutes in Rome and elsewhere.
In the same way in the field of means of communication and information, we can record the concessions given to religious communities to print locally a certain number of prayer books and catechisms, the authorization given to send some thousand religious publications (gospels, bibles, catechisms) or liturgical publications (missals, ritual for the administration of the sacraments, brevaries for priests and religious works of piety), to Catholic communities who previously could neither print nor import; furthermore, the now unhindered reception without interference for some radio religious programs, like the Radio Vatican broadcasts.
These measures, which we stress with satisfaction, correspond to commitments in the Final Act and have begun to modify-even though it is but partially so far, and not to the same extent everywhere, a previous situation which in the field of communications and relations from one country to another, was previously one of rigid and discouraging frustration.
These words are from one of the top diplomats at the Holy See who commented in October, 1977, at Belgrade about the progress being made there in terms of religious freedom. They are by an individual who certainly has a much greater understanding than the one displayed by the spokesmen for the official opposition this afternoon on the complexity of this issue and the slowness with which this progress has to take place.
One would imagine that the Leader of the Opposition or the right hon. member for Prince Albert expected the day after the signing of the Helsinki Agreement an immediate change, from night to day, in the conditions prevailing in the countries in eastern Europe. That is naive. I will comment later on our present approach of exercising quiet diplomacy. However, they expect there ought to be an immediate, radical, and profound change to bring about a society in those eastern countries which would adopt the same kind of values, communications and general freedoms as we know them in Canada. That is simply absurd and unreal.
I do not think the Leader of the Opposition or the right hon. member for Prince Albert achieved anything useful or substantial except increasing their electoral support in Canada by making the kind of statements they made this afternoon. That

is cheap politics, catering to the vote at home. It certainly will not earn them one bit of respect, recognition or influence in the international fora in the world outside this building and away from this Hill where we have to operate, and deal with those groups of nations of competing ideologies and competing systems.
The right hon. member for Prince Albert tried to treat us to a great performance of his own, allowing his ego to be expanded all over the place. He really did not do much service to the cause of human rights in which we definitely share. The Progressive Conservative party has no monopoly by expounding the view it has.
In concluding the first part of my remarks, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby is to be commended for approaching the matter in a cool, substantial and broad sense, not dealing with human rights in a narrow, partisan political consideration.
The Leader of the Opposition in his very excellent French made reference to le manque de volonte des dirigeants Sovie-tiques in the sense there is a lack of will on the part of the Soviet leadership in implementing the Helsinki Agreement. In that reference he also said trop de reticence de la part du gouvernement Canadien, too much reluctance on the part of the Canadian government to deal with them.
I cannot comment about the attitudes of the Soviet leaders. However, I can certainly tell hon. members, some of whom will participate in this debate, who were in Belgrade, that there was certainly no reticence on the part of the Canadian delegation and Canadian government in giving direction and inspiration from Ottawa, to our officials in Belgrade. Daily they expressed forcefully and openly our deep concern about the question of human rights and the slowness of implementation contained in the Helsinki Agreement on the part of some of the Eastern European countries.
I spent five weeks in Belgrade on the Third Basket committee which dealt with the question of human context, human exchanges, religious freedoms and all of that subject. There was not one day when the representatives of the Canadian government, through officials of External Affairs, did not hammer away at representatives of the Soviet Union, sometimes to a degree almost unusual by standards of Canadian performance in the past, persisting, protesting, and making the point about the high degree of discontent expressed by the western communities and the Canadian people about their slowness of performance, a slowness on the part of the Soviet Union and other eastern countries in coming closer to achieving the objectives contained in the Final Act.
It is easy for us to point the finger and expect more from countries which are not under our control, countries which have their own sovereignty and jurisdiction. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby stated earlier it is easy to make great speeches until one has to face the reality of an international forum.
One of the basic achievements of the Helsinki Agreement is that it is possible to bring to discussion around the bargaining table those countries with which we evidentally have ideologi-
May 31, 1978

cal disagreements, to express our criticism of their shortcomings in implementing some parts of the Act which ought to be implemented. It offers them the same opportunity. We are ourselves not entirely free of blame when it comes to the issue of human rights. We were criticized while we were there for our treatment of our native people-our shortcomings in this area were exploited to the full-and our critics were able to refer to other social shortcomings in western society. So there is an exchange of views and, at the same time, I believe, there is a slow but progressive move toward liberalization and the implementation of some of the basic freedoms in which the world of public opinion so largely believes.
One thing became evident in those days in Belgrade. It is that the eastern European countries are not wholly insensitive to world opinion, as may sometimes seem to be the case from here. They are concerned about it and they try, either by cover-up tactics, to answer criticism or, at least, to give the impression that they are above criticism. Whether we can bring them to our standards and to the implementation of the basic principles in which we believe, in a matter of years or decades, is a big question. 1 believe it is a matter of decades, because it is hard to expect that monolithic systems which for centuries have been based on a different theory of government can quickly accept an entirely different approach to the role of the citizen, of the judiciary, and of the state.
We have been accused of lack of will to play a leading role in securing human rights. This view was expressed by the Leader of the Opposition. If the hon. gentleman wants proof of the kind of role we played in Belgrade I would urge him to read extracts from the speeches and interventions made by Canadian representatives between October, 1977, and March, 1978. They are in print. They have been published by the Department of External Affairs, and they give a wide-ranging sample of major interventions on the part of Canada. These extracts should be enough to show that we did, in fact, play a leading role, making our views known at every opportunity. The booklet to which I have just referred contains only excerpts from speeches and contributions made during plenary sessions; it contains no record of Canadian interventions during meetings of the committees which were held every day-it would take an encyclopedia to incorporate all of those. Nevertheless, it was in committee we were most vocal and determined to play precisely the kind of role the opposition accuses us of failing to play.
Critics of Canada's diplomacy should ask themselves which is likely to be the more productive, the quiet diplomacy or the strident kind, the kind of diplomacy which attempts to get the best possible deal from other countries or that which is designed to go down well at home.
