speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to join in this debate on the motion introduced by the hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark). The motion of the hon. member deals with a very touchy subject in which I have been interested for quite some time. The violations of human rights in the world are a major obstacle to the harmonious development of the nations and co-operation between them. A long time before the conclusion of the Helsinki Final Act came the UN Universal Charter of Human Rights.
When looking briefly at the tense situation which is developing today just about everywhere in the world and where on a daily basis individuals are denied their fundamental liberties, we realize that these beautiful resolutions still have to be implemented. People had hoped that after the signing of the Final Act of Helsinki detente between the two blocs would become a reality for all their citizens. The final act is rather clear on that issue. All participating states are bound to respect human rights and fundamental liberties such as freedom of thought, of conscience, of religion and of political persuasion. The signatory states are also supposed to favour and encourage the effective practice of civil and political rights, as well as economic, social and cultural rights as well as others which pertain to human dignity. What have the Soviet bloc nations done to implement this act to which they have subscribed? Newspapers keep reporting violations of the Helsinki accords by the Soviet Union and Czechoslovakia. And there are still many cases that will never be known to the press.
The Belgrade conference which followed the Helsinki conference and which was to consider the progress made since the Final agreement was signed was a monumental farce. It became quite obvious that that conference was going nowhere. Every intervention in favour of the upholding of human rights in the Soviet Union was seen by Moscow representatives as interference in their internal affairs. Mr. Speaker, must we remain insensitive to citizens being denied their basic rights simply because they do not live here? Should we close our eyes to the massacres in Uganda, the military regimes in Africa and Latin America, the racist regime in South Africa? No, Mr. Speaker. Human rights are the responsibility of all conscious citizens in the whole world. There is in Czechoslovakia a movement called Charter 77 which was formed by individuals concerned with the indifference of their government vis-a-vis the Helsinki Accords.
Those individuals monitor the implementation of the principles in the final act in their country. It is through that association that the foreign press can get information on the situation with respect to human rights in eastern countries. In a recent document, the spokesmen for Charter 77 show that in that country which is signatory to the Helsinki agreement, nearly 30,000 persons are placed in preventive custody every year. And I did say, Mr. Speaker, in preventive custody. They are locked up before they criticize the regime out loud. A

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
recent piece of news informed us that many known signatories to that charter are arrested without any other form of trial and bullied during questionings.
Another recent event took place in the Soviet Union. Physicist Youri Orlov was sentenced to seven years in labour camp and five years in exile. The only thing they could find against Mr. Orlov was being the leader of the Helsinki group which was trying to monitor the implementation of the Helsinki agreements in the U.S.S.R. Mr. Orlov is only the last of several Soviet dissidents who cherish human rights and have all been sentenced to maximum penalties. Earlier this month, in Rostov, 2,000 Baptists were detained following a religious demonstration. And what about the inhuman situations that Soviet Jews must endure before emigrating to Israel? Those people must wait years, lose all their rights and belongings before being able to leave that country in very small numbers.
In light of that situation and the obvious repression that exists in the U.S.S.R. and Czechoslovakia there is no protest from this government. Can we accfept, Mr. Speaker, that our government should remain quiet in face of those flagrant violations of human rights and the brutality to which dissidents are submitted?
It is true that lately, given such bills as the legislation on mail interception, the performance of the government concerning human rights is rather inadequate. In the introduction of a booklet entitled "Canada at Belgrade," the Secretary of State for External Affairs said about the preliminary steps to the conclusion of the Helsinki Final Act and I quote:
Canada was particularly active in promoting the practical down-to-earth expressions of human rights, such as the freer movement of people and the freer flow of ideas.
In the present situation, Mr. Speaker, the minister should have said instead that Canada was particularly passive in promoting the practical down-to-earth expressions of human rights. Apparently the government is not overly concerned about those rights. It is true that with the sales tax issue we forgot some very important problems. We must recognize that if some freedoms are endangered in the world, they are our owns.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, let me repeat the advice I gave to the people of the Dominion of Canada English Speaking Association who sent me a document in which they asked for the abolition of French language rights in Canada. In a letter published by the newspaper Le Droit, two weeks ago I said:
As long as there are language barriers and as long as any one of us suffers from discrimination because his language is not that of the majority or because he is different from those who consider themselves as the sole depositaries of truth and right, none of us can really be sure about his already limited freedoms.
The government should implement the principle that man is there to be loved. Dignity is to be the object of unconditional love.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) would like to contribute to this debate, and I will cut my remarks short so that he will have at least half the time which might be available to both of us before the end of this debate.
I want to say at the outset that in a debate as important as this it is only natural for those of us who live in political life to become involved in a political way, but the reason of a person such as myself for trying to insist on the timing of speeches in this debate was to ensure that it might be possible that the two final speakers, in this case the hon. member for Grey-Simcoe and myself, might be able to speak.
I remember as a young Canadian considering the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) to be an outstanding Prime Minister in the area of human rights. I also remember that in his day the late Right Hon. Lester Pearson was also considered to be a man who made great contributions at the United Nations regarding human rights. I think it is rather unfortunate and unexpected that in a matter as important as this, regardless of political feelings-and we may disagree on methods-that some do not recognize that in his speeches in the last few days on disarmament and NATO, which are not unrelated to this matter, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) put Canada in the forefront, and Canadian policy in the forefront, regarding human rights. I think that should be accepted and understood clearly.
In his speech on disarmament at the United Nations the Prime Minister said, and I quote:
I believe world security would be seriously diminished by the further spread of nuclear weapons and that it is the responsible course for governments to pursue policies based on the presumption that proliferation can be stopped.
There have been innuendoes today that the Prime Minister has not said anything against the neutron bomb. He has indicated clearly his desire that this kind of build-up should not occur. This is closely associated with human rights, because if a neutron bomb were dropped here today, the desks would be here, the lights would be here, the cameras would be here, and the building would be here, but we would not. Not even a fly would be here. The neutron bomb is an attack on life itself. It is not a simple war weapon, and therefore when we deal with disarmament we are dealing with something which vitally involves human rights. When we deal with NATO, we are involved with the same thing.
The Prime Minister has also pointed out that when we talk about security and security of individuals and nations, we have to realize that those nations in the so-called atomic pact feel the necessity to create balances for their security. Others who are involved with conventional arms feel the necessity of having 30,000 tanks for security. Others feel they need 20,000 aircraft for security. Those of us who want disarmament are apprehensive about the security of all those who live on this planet, and therefore we want a reduction in arms.

May 31, 1978

We cannot achieve security by telling others that they should not have concern about their security. Sometimes our stand in NATO should be that we must together be certain that we are adequately armed for security purposes, but our stance in the United Nations must sometimes also be that we should achieve some methods whereby we can stop further development of weapons and then begin to disarm. It was a dream after the first world war. It was a dream at Geneva. This is the first time someone has tried to revive that dream in the presence of all nations. It is an important dream. If we remember that it is a political dream, then we can move into the arena of civil rights. We must understand that the armed forces and those matters of defence and security are arms of political policy which do not in themselves make political policy.
Perhaps the Prime Minister does not speak in the same manner as members of the opposition parties or other members of parliament. But he is speaking as most Canadians and most members of parliament want him to speak. We speak for disarmament. We speak for security for ourselves. We speak and have concern for the human rights of others. The first time the Prime Minister spoke at the United Nations, he brought forth a concrete suggestion as to how we might proceed with concern. He brought forth the so-called strategy of suffocation.

I should like to remind the hon. member that this is not something to laugh at. At least it is a starting point. Referring to the neutron bomb and its attack on life, we say that there should be a completely agreed upon test ban. Why? Because we cannot stop minds from thinking, scientists from working, or laboratory work. If we have a test ban, the work of scientists is confined to laboratories. They cannot go out and do repeated tests in an attempt to discover a weapon greater than the neutron bomb. The test ban is very important. At least it will keep the control of new developments in the laboratories.
A second area involved in the strategy of suffocation, or putting the lid on the jar, is to place a ban on the flight testing of vehicles which deliver weapons. Both of these points are terribly important to the world. That fact can be verified. We must be honest about it. It is a fact that we trust each other and we love each other. All God's children love each other, but all God's children usually check on each other. We must attempt to do these things together. We can check flight testing of vehicles and flight delivery systems. Those two things are possible in this world.
Also we should check the distribution of material for war use. We can check the actual production and development of new weapons. If we check those three areas, the further production of war instruments which would be an attack on life itself can be suffocated.
Human Rights
The fourth proposition is an interesting one. We must look at the actual expenses each country puts into the production of nuclear devices for war. If an institution were set up in order to study matters in a world-like manner, we would be aware of what each country puts into that segment known as its so-called security. Then we would be placed in a position where we could say: is this reasonable for the Soviet Union, for the United States, or for Canada?
Canada is a country of many capabilities. It has had a series of governments. 1 have respect for hon. members opposite. All Canadians are the same. Canada has not developed atomic warfare weapons on its soil. We made that choice. I doubt whether any political party would come forward and indicate that we should. Through the expense strategy, we could suffocate further the greater development of atomic weapons. That is the first step. It must be followed by a more major step which is closer to the area of civil rights.
Civil rights seem to be impinged on by more conventional ideas. They are dealt with by people with conventional weapons. They come in the midst of the night and knock on doors. They take people to prisons and torture them. They do not allow people to speak out concerning their opinions. If we can arrive at some agreement in the first area, then we could reach the conventional area.
Since 1945 there have been 135 or 138 conflicts. Approximately 80 countries have been involved in these conflicts. As a result of them, 25 million people have died. Not one atomic bomb has been dropped. Thus, those people have been killed by conventional weapons, or perhaps they have been secreted away somewhere.
At this time we are involved in a debate which I hope will continue. I hope the young are attracted to this issue. I hope it is discussed in our schools. It is at the very root of Canada's destiny. They should listen to the attitude we portray to the world, as well as what is said of import.
During the great days of the Japanese they developed printed circuits, small radios, and technical equipment which became so important to us. At the same time, the Americans and Russians sent people to the moon. Because of our attitudes and the kind of people we are, perhaps we will solve our own differences of opinion. Perhaps we will bring forth new fathers of confederation and a new constitution. Perhaps we will bring forth new ideas on disarmament, civil rights and attitudes. Perhaps attitude is the great export Canada has to offer to the world. This is an important chance for us.
We must remember the time when Portia White was turned away from places in Canada. She was a beautiful contralto, a beautiful singer from Halifax. She was a beautiful negro woman who was turned away. We must remember Marian Anderson who was not allowed to stay at the Royal York Hotel when she was speaking at a Canadian Club luncheon. We must remember North Hatley in Quebec with its signs which read: "Dogs and Jews not admitted, Christians only". Those of us who lived in Canada and were required to face those things understand what human rights are all about. We have a right to change such attitudes. We are far ahead in our

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
own freedoms, but we must not forget that Belgrade is far more important to the mothers, fathers, brothers, sisters and relatives in Canada who have families elsewhere in the world who are much more maligned than us.
The motion before us is an important one. Although it tends to be critical of the government, its aim is to get at the fact that something must be done about human rights in the world. Are we going to do something? We must have good discussions on this. We should remember that we have a good Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). He is capable of speaking well, logically, solidly, and honestly on this subject. He would have participated in this debate if it had not been necessary for him to go to Washington. He is in Washington facing another phase of civil rights in the NATO meetings. We should remember that we have a Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Cafik). By taking on that portfolio, he stands for all the ethno-cultural groups in Canada. Automatically he must associate himself with the hopes, aspirations, and loves of those people for their loved ones in other countries.
All of us should remember that we can make our lives sublime, as great men in history have done. The footprints of Canada in the sands of time must be strong. We must be prepared to put our lives forward for the lives of brothers and sisters in Europe, Asia, Russia or Africa. Canada must play its role in the world. We must come forward to be counted.
The Prime Minister, the cabinet, government members, opposition members and senators, as a federation must guarantee the human rights and the dignity of individuals. Human rights are important. We must support disarmament, because the newest development is an attack on life itself. We should do something to improve this planet for our existence, and then move on to social and political problems which will be even more difficult.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. MacFarlane) for being courteous by allowing me some of his allotted time in order to participate in this very important subject this afternoon.
I think, Mr. Speaker, as others have already said, that the subject of human rights and the concern that all of us in this House 1 am sure have regarding this important issue, are far too important to be the subject of political partisanship, but instead should be an all embracing concern for all of us in parliament if we are ever to be successful is not only guaranteeing and upholding the human rights of every individual in Canada but, equally important, in our universal fight to uphold the sacred human rights of all human beings in every corner of the world as well.
Having said that, I have to say 1 was greatly disappointed and dismayed by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) who, instead of trying to make a contribution to this very important discussion here this afternoon, chose to use most of

his time in berating and highly criticizing the contributions of others members of the House who participated in this debate in good faith and with an earnest desire to seek progress in our constant fight to improve the progress of human rights throughout the globe. 1 am sure this type of diplomacy, as exhibited here this afternoon, would have a very low priority in discussions of human rights, or in any other discussions, for that matter.
Canadians as a race, 1 think, are inclined to be complacent about human rights. We are even more inclined to forget that we have some responsibility for what is happening in other parts of the world and that what is happening in other parts of the world can and does affect the kind of life we can live here in Canada.
At times we take for granted our basic human rights; freedom of speech, freedom of the press, freedom to worship, and even a right to a certain standard of living. These are accepted without question. It is not always easy for Canadians to comprehend the harsh realities of life in Eastern Europe where about 300 million people languish under an oppressive police rule, their families are held hostage, their freedom of movement is curtailed, and no aspect of their lives is without surveillance of some sort.
Several years ago the Helsinki conferences were convened in an attempt to promote detente in Europe and to reach some sort of international consensus on the recognition of human liberties and rights. The rights of individuals, families and cultures were explicitly recognized by the 35 signatories to the Helsinki Agreement.
The recent review of the implementation of the Helsinki pact has made clear that the Soviet Union and its satellites are not living up to their promise to observe in practice those principles set out at Helsinki.
Anxious to secure the legitimization of its post-war boundaries, the Soviet Union was perfectly willing to give voice to its support for human rights. In action, however, it deliberately and systematically falls short. Numerous violations of the Helsinki accords are now coming to light, the most recent involving the sentencing of Yuri Orlov, who was tried and convicted for the so-called crime of monitoring the Soviet Union's human rights performance against the pledge made in Helsinki.
The Nobel prize winner Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn, Amnesty International, the Samizdat Sources, the ever increasing number of dissidents in the Soviet Union, and various publications in the west, have well documented the suppression of liberty and the gross violation of human rights within the U.S.S.R. and its controlled satellite countries. All along, the Soviets have insisted upon their right to do as they please on their own home territory. However, the gross and systematic violation of human rights must be regarded as an international concern and no longer as the exclusive preserve of the domestic jurisdiction of the country concerned.
The approach of the government with respect to this issue has been, on the whole, one of quiet diplomacy. Apparently the
May 31, 1978

government hopes that by means of behind the scenes negotiations it will be able to influence the policies of the Eastern bloc countries on such issues as family reunification, freedom of movement, and the unjust imprisonment of Soviet dissidents. The over-all results have been less than satisfactory.
Yuri Orlov is only one of several dissidents who have been harassed or imprisoned this past year for attempting to monitor the Soviet government's performance under the Helsinki Accord. Though it has become somewhat easier for a westerner to travel in the Soviet Union, the movement of Soviet citizens is still severely restricted, and the whole question of family reunification is far from resolved.
The Canadian Ukrainian Immigrant Aid Society, in cooperation with the Department of External Affairs, recently undertook a project of conducting a Canada-wide compilation and analysis of the reunification problem. The results indicated that in the majority of cases there has not been settlement for periods of over 30 years and, in many instances, for over 50 years. Most tragic of all is the length of time involved. Many have been attempting to reunify immediate families for over a quarter of a century, and some for half a century.
It is time our government took a more vocal and outspoken position. It is apparent that the situation will not be solved through the use of regular bureaucratic channels, or by so-called quiet diplomacy.
To effect change, the violations of the Helsinki Accord must be brought to public awareness, for in the present state of international law on human rights the most effective sanction is the force of international public opinion, which is something to which even the most authoritarian governments are sensitive.
"Public opinion is the most powerful medium of all. Like religion it penetrates into the darkest corners." That is from a letter written over 150 years ago by Metternich, the authoritarian Austrian foreign minister.
I have another quotation also from a source not usually associated with concern for human rights. It is from the Wall Street Journal and states:
There is little question that the dissidents have been able to survive as they have because people abroad were listening to them.
That was in reference to Soviet dissidents.
The point is that an outspoken and vocal condemnation of the violation of human rights will have more effect than a policy of quiet diplomacy in arousing public opinion and putting pressure on Soviet authorities.
Undoubtedly, Canadians have a lot to be thankful for. Canada is a far cry from being a police state. However, can we really settle back in our chairs secure in the knowledge that Canada is a true democracy where social, economic, political, and cultural rights are fully respected? 1 would suggest that we cannot afford to get too complacent. One has only to read the daily press to realize that Canada has its own problems in the area of human rights.
Human Rights
Of course infringements on civil and human liberties in Canada are not nearly as severe as in the Soviet bloc countries. However, our own failings will have to be faced and dealt with if we are going to accept the task of acting as watchdogs over human rights in the rest of the world.
Canadians have achieved equality before the law, but in reality we fall far short of reaching the ideal of democratic freedoms. Incidents of racism and discrimination are growing at an alarming rate. It was for this reason the House felt compelled to pass a human rights act setting out the prohibited grounds of discrimination. The House also passed legislation to establish a commission to monitor the implementation of the Human Rights Act.
Unfortunately, no government can legislate away racism or discrimination. Human rights and human dignity in Canada, as elsewhere in the world, have not been and are not likely to be realized by lofty rhetoric even when enshrined in a constitution. The only way they can be achieved is by those relentless forces of social change, and by our timely response to them. It is a question of giving substance to words, by taking positive and constructive action in order to attempt to create a climate in which racism and discrimination will not flourish.
In Canada a concept of cultural pluralism and human rights is being encouraged and actively pursued in the belief that our society will become stronger and more enriched. There is no doubt about the realism of the concept. However, to attain that goal we have to translate that concept into practice. Action, not empty words or empty promises, is the course we have to take if we are really sincere in the building of our nation. It is for this reason that I support a multiculturalism policy for Canada.
I have no hesitation in stating that multiculturalism is the most suitable way of assuring not only cultural freedom but all our basic human liberties in every corner of our country. A recognition of multiculturalism in Canada assures that ethnic groups in Canada will be guaranteed their right and desire to practise and keep their traditions, language, and culture.
The universal acceptance of multiculturalism in Canada by all its citizens will mean, as well, greater respect and understanding of each other. It will also mean the disappearance of personal and institutional prejudices and the creation of a more friendly and open climate. Without the eradication of the disease of prejudice and racism, no basic human rights will ever be a reality in Canada and we will never earn the title of a truly great nation.
Because I feel so strongly about the value of a multiculturalism policy as a means to enhance human rights and human dignity, I cannot help but be very concerned about the manner in which it is being implemented by this government. It is apparent that the government is far from committed to a multicultural Canadian society, despite any outcry to the contrary. The government's hesitation to commit itself has been illustrated on a number of occasions. For instance, since the announcement of the policy in October, 1971, there have
5940

May 31, 1978
Human Rights
been only two full time ministers for multiculturalism, and both of these appointments were made when an election appeared imminent. That alone should indicate the lack of priority that this government gives to multiculturalism in Canada.
The recent announcement of an increase in the multiculturalism budget is undoubtedly another attempt on the part of the government to endear itself to the ethnocultural communities just prior to an election. The government has announced that the multiculturalism budget will amount to $50 million over the next five years. This sum sounds like a lot of money until it is broken down by year. The government is telling us that the multiculturalism budget will now be $10 million per year, an actual increase of slightly less than $2 million per year over the present budget.
It was something like four years ago that this government first promised to increase the multiculturalism budget to $10 million annually. It has taken the government four years, and the possibility of another election, to reiterate this promise, and from the experiences of four years ago we know there is no guarantee the government will keep this promise.
In view of the present spending practices of the multiculturalism directorate, we can expect at least 40 per cent, or $4 million, to be used on advertising and administrative expenses. A further $3 million will be spent by the cultural agencies such as the National Film Board and the Museum of Man. That leaves roughly $3 million to be used directly by the ethno-cultural communities for language and culture retention, not a very large sum when you consider that the government plans to spend $4.5 million alone in one week of Canada Day celebrations. When you consider that our ethno-cultural communities-and I am referring to those who have neither French nor English as their background-represent more than one third of the population of Canada, a budget of $10 million annually is an effrontery of the first magnitude.
Last summer the government had an opportunity to make a positive contribution to the development of the multicultural ideal in Canada, an opportunity which it failed to take advantage of. At that time a motion was introduced to amend the Immigration Act so that it could take into consideration not only the bilingual character of Canadian society but also its multicultural nature. We on this side of the House supported the motion which gave recognition to the fact that Canada is composed of many different ethnocultural groups which want to cherish their different cultures without penalty, and which want to feel they are co-equals in the building and development of Canadian society. The motion, however, was defeated by government members in the House, raising serious doubts about the sincerity of the government's intentions with respect to multiculturalism.
In view of the government's noncommital attitude, it is not surprising that many Canadians are still unfamiliar with the goals of multiculturalism policy. A recently published majority
attitudes study revealed that most Canadians were really unaware of a multiculturalism policy in Canada, and those who were aware of such a policy perceived it only in the context of allowing immigrants to maintain their customs and folk traditions. It is apparent that a great deal more effort must be made before a policy of multiculturalism moves beyond indifferent acceptance to understanding and use by all Canadians regardless of their ethnic origin.
It is the belief of our party that the key to a more dynamic multiculturalism policy lies in placing more decision making responsibility with the ethnocultural communities in Canada. A first step in this direction could be achieved by changing the method of selection of the representatives to the Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism. At present the members of the council are political appointments of the government. In our opinion, this is wrong. These people should be elected from the ethno-cultural communities they represent.
It is also our belief that more of an effort has to be made to try to follow through on the recommendations of the Consultative Council on Multiculturalism. Up until now the recommendations of the council have frequently been ignored, probably gathering dust in some obscure corner of the directorate. For instance, the council has repeatedly stressed the pivotal relationship of language to culture retention, recommending on several occasions that the government initiate federal-provincial agreements to introduce third language instruction in the public schools system. Needless to say, these recommendations have been largely ignored by the government.
From its inception, the council has also recommended that the mandate of the CBC be revised so as to allow for the introduction of multilingual broadcasting, but so far the results have not been very encouraging. The council further recommended that all federal cultural agencies include qualified persons of various ethno-cultural backgrounds on their governing boards.
A multiculturalism policy, to be successful, must take into consideration a broad spectrum of society, including education, the broadcasting media, newspapers and literature, the performing arts, museum programs, community cultural centres, government services, youth programs, and relations with other countries. Above all, if we are concerned with changing attitudes in Canada, then multiculturalism must be a predominant theme in the education system. From the beginning of Confederation, Mr. Speaker, cultural and linguistic questions have always been central to Canada's existence as a unified and civilized nation.
